title: Brother of Edmonton man shot and killed by Edmonton police files $130,000 lawsuit against city
article: The brother of an Edmonton man who was shot dead by police has launched a $130,000 lawsuit against the City of Edmonton and the officer who shot him.

According to a statement of claim filed in Court of Queen's Bench on March 15, Ira Bitternose alleges the injuries to and subsequent death of Kinling Robin Fire, 39, were the result of negligence by the officer involved.

Bitternose claims the officer failed to operate his handgun in accordance with EPS policy and procedure or with due care and attention and he generally failed to carry out his duties in a reasonable manner.
According to the statement of claim, Fire became involved in a dispute with his estranged common-law wife over custody of their son about 11 p.m. on March 30, 2011.
The dispute ended with Fire leaving his west-end apartment building in his vehicle.
The common-law wife called 911 and, just after midnight, Fire was apprehended by three police officers as he drove into the parking lot behind his apartment building.

Bitternose alleges an altercation broke out between Fire and the three officers and one of the officers drew his gun and shot Fire two times, hitting him in the chest and stomach. He died from his injuries in hospital later that day.
Bitternose is seeking $10,000 to cover the costs of funeral related expenses and $120,000 in damages for bereavement on behalf of Fire's parents and his three children.
A statement of defence has not yet been filed. Statements of claim and statements of defence contain allegations which have not been proven in court.

Meanwhile, an investigation into the shooting by the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team concluded in July that no charges would be laid against the officer who fired the fatal shots due to him believing that he was in a life-threatening situation and his life was in danger.
According to the investigation, police boxed in Fire's vehicle and attempted to get him to come out of it. He eventually did, but had a steel bar in his possession.
One of the three officers tried to use his patrol car to knock Fire to the ground. He wasn't injured and got up and ran towards an officer standing outside his vehicle.

"The man advanced on police while being directed to stop and drop his weapon, but he refused to do so," said ASIRT executive director Clif Purvis, noting Fire was still fighting when police were placing him under arrest.
